prize_parts.citation: for a visionary body of prose, rooted in his poetry, in which memory, the body and cosmology are fused into a singular, densely patterned metaphysical imaginative architecture

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change, but the grounds are narrower and more carefully stated after the exchange. Cărtărescu's case rests on a voice that is recognisable at the level of the paragraph, on the formal ambition of building memory, the body, dream and cosmology into recursive prose, and on a project carried through several very large books over decades. On public knowledge, the Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy works from childhood, the body and inherited memory, and Solenoid, as I understand it, shifts to an adult narrator and a different metaphysical premise. If that is right, it is a new formal problem and not a replay of the earlier books. That is the best evidence I can offer for development over repetition, and I flag it as public knowledge, not verified reading. In response to the chair's question about scope, I now favour a citation anchored in the major prose with the poetry named as its origin. I do not claim the whole oeuvre equally, because the poetry and early work are thinner in the translations we can assess. The attribution is clean: one writer, one language, no dependence on national or political symbolism. The unanimity of the opening rankings is not literary evidence. I rely on voice, form and sustained depth, which are the common criteria.
statement.case_against: I take the chair's request seriously that someone argue the strongest case against Cărtărescu. It runs as follows. The committee is judging largely through translation a writer whose force may lie in Romanian sentence rhythm, wordplay and syntactic patterning. Without a Romanian-language reading we may be rewarding the translated architecture and reputation of the books, not the writing itself. Recurrent motifs across very long books may be a closed circuit and not an expanding world, and the reorganisation of the same materials at different scales, which Sem-Sandberg reads as development, could equally be variation within one idea. Some of the largest books may be uneven in control. I also need to correct something from round 1. I suggested that Cărtărescu's effect survives translation better than Michon's because it depends on architecture and imagery more than on cadence. That is a judgment about the type of effect, not a verified claim, and Carlberg and Olsson are right that his long, patterned sentences also depend on rhythm. If a Romanian-language assessment showed material flattening, the case would weaken and Michon or Can Xue would need real reconsideration. They carry their own translation and corpus-coverage limits.

responses.point: Olsson names recurrent motifs as the real test of Cărtărescu's candidacy (a unified world or a closed circuit), says the answer must come from the books and not their reputation, and notes that uneven coverage of the poetry argues for a citation grounded mainly in the major prose with the poetry as a related strand.
responses.response: I agree, and I have changed my citation wording accordingly: it now names the prose as the body of work and the poetry as its root. On the test itself, the only fair way I can see to apply it is book against book. The question is whether Solenoid poses a different formal and metaphysical problem from the Orbitor trilogy, or restates the same material in a larger frame. I believe the former from public knowledge, but I cannot settle it by assertion and I do not claim to. I also accept your caution that Carson stays open as an English-language alternative only if the Romanian cannot be judged. I do not advance her as mine, because I would still want her core literary contribution defined apart from book design, translation and scholarship.

responses.point: Mattson reads motif repetition across the large works as the means by which the project accumulates meaning, and keeps Michon as her first alternative on intensity of voice. She wants any citation to say precisely what is honoured and not rely on general stature.
responses.response: I accept that accumulation is a plausible reading, but I would not call it established. A recurring image can accumulate or merely recur, and only a close comparison of specific books can show which. On Michon we are close. I regard the voice as among the most concentrated on the list, and my alternatives still begin with him. I read the criterion of sustained achievement as asking for evidence of range, and a slim corpus gives us less of it. I would not call it a mistake if the committee judged intensity sufficient. I also share your point about precision: for Michon a citation would honour the invention of a form of fictional lives, and for Cărtărescu it should honour the prose architecture, not stature.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg argues that the major books reorganise the same materials at different scales and in different forms, which he reads as development, and he discloses his Central European engagement as thematic proximity and not a personal tie.
responses.response: Reorganisation at different scales is the strongest version of the development argument, but I would put a further question to it. Does each reorganisation create a new formal problem, or does it only enlarge the same solution? That is a distinction I cannot resolve without close comparison of books, and I would ask you which two you would set side by side. I also appreciate the transparency of your conflict note. I treat thematic proximity as a possible familiarity effect, not a reason to discount your reading, and I think the same candour should apply to my own affinity for narrative traditions.

responses.point: Carlberg keeps Carson as an alternative and suggests that a citation could be scoped around poetry and lyric-essayistic renewal, while admitting it needs more articulation than the Cărtărescu case. She also ranks Michon seventh on breadth and translation loss.
responses.response: Your suggested scope for Carson, poetry and lyric-essayistic renewal, is the most workable drafting I have seen, and it addresses part of my doubt from round 1. It still leaves my question open: how much of the achievement belongs to the text and how much to book design and classical scholarship at the edge of an original oeuvre. For that reason I keep Carson out of my two alternatives. On Michon, I accept your breadth point but would resist treating translation loss as decisive against him alone. It applies to every candidate we judge in translation, and I try to apply it to Cărtărescu as well.

responses.point: Sward holds Can Xue as an alternative on the strength of an internally rigorous dream-logic method with few parallels. She says she would want better evidence of development across a large, partly untranslated corpus before moving her above a writer whose variety is clearer to her.
responses.response: We are close here. I keep Can Xue as my second alternative for the reason you give, that the method is deliberate and not ornament. My unresolved question is also yours: whether it deepens or only repeats across the large output. I would add that the chair's request for a regional expert assessment applies to her at least as strongly as to Cărtărescu, since the translated selection may not represent the whole. I would welcome any specific later work that you or others think extends the method.

uncertainties: How much of the rhythm, wordplay and syntactic patterning of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives in the translations available to the committee. No member, myself included, claims command of the originals, and nothing here has been independently verified.

Whether Solenoid and the other late large books pose new formal and metaphysical problems relative to the Orbitor trilogy, or enlarge the same solution. My view rests on public knowledge and not on verified reading.
How much of the poetry and early work is available in translation, and so how far a citation can responsibly cover it. This is the reason I now anchor the citation in the prose.
Whether Michon's compact corpus and Can Xue's partly translated, method-driven corpus give enough evidence of range and development to rival a larger body of work.

Whether Carson's hybrid work can be scoped as an oeuvre under Nobel's will without relying on book design, translation or scholarship. For this I defer to colleagues who have studied the works more closely.

Round 1 convergence on one writer is not literary evidence and may have shortened scrutiny of shared reservations. This committee recommendation models only a single configuration and the full Swedish Academy decides the actual award.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from the supplied profile. It records no professional or personal tie to any shortlisted writer. My work as a novelist, short-story writer and Lagerlöf biographer, and my stated affinity with a British storytelling tradition, are context and not evidence of preference. I name no relationship with any shortlisted writer beyond reading the public record, and my judgments rest on public knowledge and translation, not on independent source verification. Carlberg's voting status as a co-opted member is undocumented, which is a modeling matter and not a conflict of mine.
